text:
4/1/25 Notes:
● Chicano studies: study of experiences, values, cultural
representations, socio economic issues of Chicano/Latino
community
● Chicano studies department achieved through struggle (strikes
- UC Berkeley and SF state)
● Late 60s/early 70s
○ Global decolonial movements + student protests
○ Radical movements - racial injustice
○ Critical consciousness - US racism and imperialism
○ Discontent w/gains of post-WW2 era
■ Minorities critical in helping country but - came
home thinking they would be respected and instead
were not treated as such
● Who are chicano people?
○ Empowering alternative name to hispanic, mexican, and
mexican american
○ Uplift marginalized group
○ Signal connection to indigeneity
○ Relatively unpopular among mexican americans and other
groups during 1960s and 70s
○ Leads to exclusion based on what the boundaries are
○ Some identify with term but others don’t
● Latino/a/x
○ People of Latin american origin or descent
○ Huge umbrella term
● Conditions that help us know latinidad? - main question!
● Attacks on ethnic studies
○ Movement to ban critical race theory (CRT)
○ Ban in tucson, arizona
○ 2025:
■ Diversity programs eliminated on college campuses
■ ICE - international student detainment
■ Ongoing genocide and militarism
4/8/25
● Final exam is final day of courses (not on the final exam date) -
the final exam date assignment will be an online submission
● 4 main terms from Omi and Winant: race, racialization, racial
project, racism
● Important topics from reading (Omi and Winant)
○ Race - not a set number, keeps changing
○ We assign meanings to differences in our human bodies
○ Ex. prior to 1492 there was no race, we had to create race
in some way
● Parks and rec clip - no basketball court
○ Popular sport we associate with black americans
○ Can read into it saying basically they do not want blacks in
the court
● Sorry to bother you movie clip - white voice
○ Non phenotypic marketers can also be racialized (ex. voice)
● Problematic dichotomy of thinking about race
○ Race as illusion (fake)
■ If race is not real, then racism is also not real
○ Race as essence (fact)
■ Some proveability that race is a real thing - verifiable
facts that we are humanly different and we have to
act accordingly
● Note that this justified the slavery of africans
● Race as a master category
● Racism (all quotes reference dehumanization)
○ Creates or reproduces structures of domination based on
racial significations and identities (Omi and Winant)
○ Nikhil Pal Singh quote on slides - something is extracted
for another
○ Ruth Wilson Gilmore quote on slides - exploitation of one
group; hierarchies of individuals we can see when
humanity is diminished which can justify enslavement or
death..
○ 3 dif definitions of racism - how to show you know a term
or concept?
■ Reference the quote
■ All are relatively similar
● Racial Projects
○ Instances, acts, or policies that do the act of racism
○ Ex. how you greet someone at the grocery store
○ Ex. how you read a character (terrible representation of
Latinx character)
○ Both culture and structures can be racial project (idea
from Omi and Winant)
■ Example: I really miss Oakland (“ooh oakland”)
● Oakland as a city can be racialized - black and
people of color more generally
● Be careful in oakland because it is dangerous
(jungle like) - cultural imagination that support
the idea that we need more police and need
more prisons
● Racism is reproduced - not a thing of the past
○ Example: schooling in the U.S. has reproduced racism
■ Admission of certain students: in early days if black
then cannot learn how to read
■ Who has access to quote on quote good schools and
bad schools (ex. Private schools)
■ Racially segregated schools has historically been a
racist racial project
● Taking from one and incorporating into
another
■ Racial integration has sought to be an antiracist
racial project
■ Mendez v. Westminster - 1946
■ Brown v. Board - 1954
● Unlawful to racially segregate students in
schools
● Took years and years to have black students in
all white schools
○ UCLA study
■ U.S. schools are widely racially segregated
○ Point of desegregating schools
■ Wanted more resources
■ Racism can be about resources - sending your kid to
a more predominantly white school because you
know that school will have more resources than a
school that contains only 10% white students
● Colonization, Conquest, and Resistance
○ Pre-Columbian America
■ 60-110 million people
■ Profound diversity
■ Most densely populated what is valley of Mexico
○ A world before race
■ Race as a social organization did not exist
○ The Moors in the Iberian Peninsula
■ Islamophobic and white supremist
■ Counternarrative: muslim presence and muslim
christian/jewish/pagan relationships in peninsula
● Seen as conquest (NOT reconquest)
○ Important to point this out because
reconquest would mean it actually
originally belonged to that group
○ (Re)Conquista
■ Uniting spain under catholic monarchy
■ Sets the tone of colonization
● Paying soldiers with land
● Intermarriages among the conquered
● Desire for continued war and plunder (ex.
Destroying synagogues and mosques)
○ Conquers and Race
■ Newly united spain was eager to fund conquest
■ Conquistadores were justified to kill and conquer
○ Encomienda system
■ Brutal form of indigenous enslavement and land theft
■ Racialized system of land seizure and labor control
● Race
● Growing global system (of enslavement)
○ Caste system
■ Top to bottoms:
● Peninsulares
● Criollos
● Indos and negros on bottom
■ Back doors where you can clear your bloodline, can
take some part of your family history out
○ Colonialism as a Gendered Project
■ Intermarriage is key in spanish colonialism
■ Gender and sexuality became dimensions of identity
that “are both an effect of power and a technology of
rule”
● How?
○ Effect of power: we live in an unequal
gender society where men have more
power than women; spanish colonialism is
creating a form of gender and sexuality
that is used to create this system as a form
of rule
○ Mexican War of Independence
■ 1821 - Treaty of Cordoba → make mexico independent
constitutional monarchy
■ 1823 - mexico = republic
○ Mexico- U.S. relations
■ Adamns racialized people in Mexico and Latin
America would haunt their descendants in the U.S.
well into the 21st century. Moreles vision of a
beautiful bond b/w Mexico and U.S. was doomed by
the imperatives of racial capitalism
● Slavery in full effect in this time
● U.S. economy dependent on slavery at this time
● If U.S. conquers large part of mexico (the part of
mexico that they take they will not make them
U.S. citizens)
■ Abolitionists and black freedom fighters recognized
the link between slavery and imperialism
○ Power and resistance
■ Acts of resistance and efforts towards racial justice
are as old as racism
4/10/25
● Race, racial project, racialization,
● Racial projects v. racism
○ Racial projects = racist → if creates or reproduces
structure of domination based on racial significations and
identities
○ Racism → larger matrix
● Racial hate v. racism
○ UCLA study → schools remain separated in terms of race
○ How does racism occur in liberal area?
○ Are bans on fluoride in drinking water racial projects?

Chapter 5: Probability and Simulations
1. General Addition Rule
a. P ( A U B ) = P(A) + P(B) - P (A and B)
b. If events are independent, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)
2. P( A given B) = P( A and B)/ P(B)
3. P(b given A) = P(A and B)/P(A)
4. P(A^c) = 1 - P(A) → complement rule
5. Probability of at least 1 out of some number
a. P(at least 1) = 1 - P(A^c)^some number
6. Mutually exclusive = disjoint
a. Events can’t happen together (zero chance)
b. P(A and B) = 0
7. Independent events
a. P(A given B) = P(A)
b. if two events are disjoint, they can’t be independent
8. Performing a Simulation
a. State: Ask a question of interest about some chance process
b. Plan: Describe how to use a chance device (beads, slips of paper, dice, or cards)
to imitate one repetition of the process. Tell what you will record at the end of
each repetition.
c. Do: Perform many repetitions of the simulation.
d. Conclude: Use the results of your simulation to answer the question of interest.
Chapter 6: Probability Distributions
1. Continuous random variables = take all values on an interval of numbers
2. Discrete random variables = random variables on a fixed set of values with gaps in
between
3. Mean for discrete variables (n = any number) p = respective probability for said number
a. μ = (n*p) + (n*p) + (n*p).....
4. Standard deviation for discrete variables
a. σ = √((n - μ)^2 (p)) + …..
b. Whole thing is square rooted
5. Transformations (mean)
a. μ = n * (original μ) → multiplication and/or division
b. μ = n + (original μ) → addition and/or subtraction ← different sign based on
operation
6. Transformations (standard deviation)
a. σ = n * (original σ) → multiplication and/or division ← different sign based on
operation
7. Transformations (mean) = adding/subbing 2 random variables
a. μ = μ(χ) + μ(Υ)
b. μ = μ(χ) - μ(Υ)
8. Transformations (standard deviation) = adding/subbing 2 random variables
a. σ = √(σχ)^2 + (σΥ)^2 ← same sign
b. transformations of stan dev = applies to the variance
c. Variance = (σ)^2
9. Binomial Distributions
a. Requirements:
i. Binary = have specific success and failure events
ii. Independent = trials are independent
iii. n = number (specified number of trials)
iv. p = number (probability is same throughout)
b. If requirements are met → binomial distribution
c. Equation for binomial distribution
i.
ii. k = success/fail
iii. n = number of trials
iv. p = probability
v. N k thing = nCr on calc
d. If need to do less than k
i. Do all calculations of the number below k (dont include k)
e. If need to do above k
i. Do all calculations of the number above k (dont include k)
f. Include k if specified
g. μ = ηρ
h. σ = √ηρ(1-ρ)
i. When the number of trials is large enough that both np and n(1 − p) are at least 10,
the distribution of the binomial random variable X has an approximately Normal
distribution.
j. Common application = count how many times a particular outcome comes in a
random sample from a population
10. Geometric Distribution
a. Requirements
i. Same as binomial BUT n is not specified
ii. No specific number of trials
b. If requirements are met → use geometric distribution
c. Count number of trials until get a success

text:
1: How did animal brains evolve?
Animal brains evolve by adding new features on top of the existing parts of
the brain instead of creating a new structure.
2: How does the analogy of an ice-cream cone by Linden apply to animal brain
evolution?
For each animal brain, the entire structure isn’t remade. Instead, the old parts
(the first scoops) are used and they are added on top of them to make the brain
more complex than the brain’s of their ancestor’s
3: Which part of the human brain is different from other animals and what functions
do scientists attribute to that part of the brain?
The midbrain in frogs and reptiles is their main visual center; whereas in
humans, it causes blindsight. The association cortex is the largest in humans than
any other animal, giving us a cognitive advantage.
4: Know the functions of these parts of the brain
Cerebrum- the largest part of the brain, performs the higher functions: memory,
speech, senses, emotional response
Cerebellum- movement, balance, coordination, distinguish expected from
unexpected sensations, predict the body’s next movement
Hypothalamus- homeostasis, secretion of hormones, TALE (temperature, appetite,
libido, emotion), fight or flight responses, basic social drives
Thalamus- relay station for sending sensory info to higher regions of the brain,
relays command signals from higher areas of the brain and sends out to different
pathways = activating muscles
Amygdala- emotions of fear and anger, also store memories of fear and anger (part
of the limbic system)
Hippocampus- makes memories and stores them as well, part of the limbic system
Frontal lobe- decision making, motor movement, problem-solving, movement
Occipital lobe- vision
Temporal lobe- auditory
Parietal lobe- sensory processing
4: Which brain parts comprise the Forebrain, Midbrain, and the Hindbrain?
Hindbrain: pons, medulla, cerebellum
Midbrain: superior colliculus, inferior colliculus
Forebrain: thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, cerebrum
5: What is the function of the Midbrain?
Blindsight, relaying info to the thalamus
6: What do scientists think happens at the Broca’s and Wernicke’s regions of the
brain?
Broca’s area controls speech while Wernicke’s area controls language
development and reading.
7: If shown a diagram of the brain, know to identify and label the following parts
Cerebrum
Cerebellum
Frontal lobe
Parietal lobe
Temporal lobe
Occipital lobe
Thalamus
Hypothalamus
Pons
Medulla oblongata
8: Which lobes have the motor cortex and the somatosensory cortex?
Parietal lobe = somatosensory cortex
Frontal lobe = motor cortex
9: Where would one find the central and lateral sulcus?
Central sulcus divides the frontal and parietal lobes, it’s between the
somatosensory cortex and motor cortex. Lateral sulcus splits up the temporal and
the parietal lobes
10: Know to identify and label the different parts of a neuron. Also, write down the
functions of each of the parts
Dendrites- branches leading into the cell body, receive info from other neurons
Cell Body- soma, where normal functions of cells take place
Axon Hillock- cone-shaped structure at the start of the axon, where the action
potential starts
Axon- long extension, transmits the signal to other neurons and carries signal across
neuron
Myelin sheath- cells that insulate the axon to speed up the action potential
Nodes of Ranvier- areas of the axon that are not insulated by myelin sheaths, where
action potentials are formed
Axon Terminal- transmit the signal across the synapse to the dendrites of the next
neuron
Synapse- space between the axon terminal and postsynaptic membrane
11: What are graded potentials?
Graded potentials are changes in polarization whose magnitude changes
based on the strength of the stimulus
12: How are action potentials generated?
by an influx of sodium ions into the cell membrane, causing the overall charge
of the intracellular side of the membrane to be positive
13: What is the resting potential of the neuron?
-70mV
14: What would happen to the resting potential if sodium ions leaked in?
it becomes positive
15: What would happen to the resting potential if potassium ions leaked out?
negative
16: What is meant by depolarization, repolarization, hyperpolarization?
depolarization = the increase of voltage to positive; sodium goes in the cell
repolarization = the decrease of voltage to negative; potassium goes out
hyperpolarization = extreme decrease of voltage (undershoot); a lot of
potassium ions go out → more than necessary
17: Will rate of impulse conduction be affected by the width of a nerve?
yes, the greater the width, the faster the impulse conduction
18: What is saltatory conduction?
saltatory conduction is a faster way to send the impulse to the next neuron by
the axon being myelinated.
19: How do the sodium channel and potassium channel proteins work? Does sodium
go in or out of the neuron through the leak channels? What about potassium?
the sodium and potassium channels are specific to a particular ion. both
sodium and potassium channels are slow to open. The channels send the ions down
their concentration gradient (areas of high concentration to areas of low
concentration). Sodium goes into the cell (since there are more sodium ions
concentrated outside the cell membrane) and potassium goes out (since there are
more ions concentrated inside the cell membrane) SALTY BANANA
20: How does the sodium/potassium pump work?
The pump takes 3 sodium ions from the intracellular fluid to change the
shape of the pump. To allow the pump to function, ATP gives up one of its
phosphates to power the pump. This allows the sodium to go out of the cell. The
pump takes in 2 potassium ions from the extracellular fluid and then changes shape
again. The pump lets the potassium go in the cell. The pump sends ions against their
concentration gradient (areas of low concentration to areas of high concentration).
21: What happen when an action potential is generated?
When the action potential is generated, the voltage is repolarized by sending
potassium ions out. That section where the action potential occurred will then
activate the action potential in the next section of the axon. The signal will then be
transmitted along the axon in this manner while the parts of the axon that received
the action potentials will be repolarized back to their resting potential.
22: Sequence the steps at the synapse starting from when an action potential
reaches the presynaptic axon terminal to the initiation of the graded potential in the
dendrite of the postsynaptic neuron?
1) Action potential reaches the axon terminals
2) Voltage-gated calcium channels open
3) the influx of calcium ions cause the synaptic vesicles, carrying the
neurotransmitters, to fuse with the presynaptic membrane
4) the neurotransmitters are then released into the synaptic cleft
5) the neurotransmitters bind to the receptor proteins on the postsynaptic
membrane
6) this allows the influx of sodium ions, generating an action potential
23: What does the neurotransmitter do in the synaptic cleft?
The neurotransmitter binds to the protein receptor on the postsynaptic
membrane to allow the influx of sodium ions into the next neuron.
24: What is the role of glutamate and GABA in the brain?
GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that stops the action potential.
Glutamate is an excitatory neurotransmitter that allows the passage of the action
potential to other neurons.
25: What happens to the neurotransmitters after the impulse has passed?
the neurotransmitters will be degraded by an enzyme, diffuse out of the
synaptic cleft, or recycled to be used again later.
